# When It Fails: Generalization in Pictures, and Inductive Bias {#sec-06-generalization-inductive-bias}

We now have
[expressive models](03-nonlinearity-mlp.qmd#sec-03-nonlinearity-mlp),
[likelihood-derived losses](02-logistic-softmax.qmd#sec-02-logistic-softmax),
[an optimizer that scales](04-training-loss-sgd.qmd#sec-04-training-loss-sgd), and
[an efficient way to compute gradients](05-backpropagation.qmd#sec-05-backpropagation).
Applied to Fashion-MNIST, this machinery reaches respectable accuracy on held-out
validation images.

Yet a validation score only estimates performance under the original
data-generating distribution. It does not tell us which transformations of the
data the classifier will tolerate. A small shift, for example, preserves the
garment's visual identity, so we expect a robust model to keep its prediction. A
complete pixel scramble, by contrast, destroys the two-dimensional spatial
arrangement; requiring a model to preserve its output under arbitrary scrambling is
neither expected nor desirable. Task-relevant invariance is selective: an image
model should tolerate nuisance displacements while remaining sensitive to the
spatial structure that defines an object.

We compare these transformations under two protocols: evaluating an already
trained model on transformed inputs, and retraining on transformed data. The
distinction separates the behavior of a particular fitted model from the
symmetries of its model family. It also motivates the locality and weight
sharing developed in Part II.

## The baseline fit: empirical risk and clean validation

We use a subset of Fashion-MNIST, a classic benchmark of 28×28 grayscale images of
clothing in ten classes. The model and training loop come from earlier chapters: we
train an MLP from @sec-03-nonlinearity-mlp exactly as in @sec-04-training-loss-sgd:

:::: {.plan-code .plan-code-wide}
::: {.plan}
1. Load and flatten the Fashion-MNIST subset, split off 200 validation images, and
   import `fit_supervised`.
2. Define the reusable helpers: `train_mlp` and `accuracy`.
3. Fit the @sec-04-training-loss-sgd recipe on the fixed Fashion-MNIST development split.
4. Print the train and validation accuracy.
:::

```{python}
#| label: victory
#| code-fold: false
import torch
from torch import nn

# [1]
torch.manual_seed(6050)
development = torch.load("../../data/fashion-train.pt")
holdout = torch.load("../../data/fashion-test.pt")
X_dev = development["X"].float().reshape(-1, 784) / 255.0  # (1200, 784)
y_dev, classes = development["y"], development["classes"]
X_test = holdout["X"].float().reshape(-1, 784) / 255.0     # (600, 784)
y_test = holdout["y"]

split = torch.randperm(len(X_dev), generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(6050))
fit_idx, val_idx = split[:1000], split[1000:]
X_tr, y_tr = X_dev[fit_idx], y_dev[fit_idx]                 # (1000, 784), (1000,)
X_val, y_val = X_dev[val_idx], y_dev[val_idx]               # (200, 784), (200,)

from dlbook.supervised import fit_supervised   # Listing 4.1
torch.set_num_threads(4)  # pinned: results depend on the CPU thread count

# [2]
def train_mlp(
    X: torch.Tensor, y: torch.Tensor, hidden: int = 256,
    epochs: int = 40, seed: int = 6050
) -> nn.Module:
    # The delta from Listing 4.1 is one line: this chapter's model.
    return fit_supervised(
        lambda: nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(784, hidden), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hidden, 10)
        ),
        X, y, epochs=epochs, seed=seed,
    )

def accuracy(net: nn.Module, X: torch.Tensor, y: torch.Tensor) -> float:
    net.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        return (net(X).argmax(1) == y).float().mean().item()

# [3]
net = train_mlp(X_tr, y_tr)
# [4]
print(f"train accuracy: {accuracy(net, X_tr, y_tr):.1%}")
print(f"validation accuracy: {accuracy(net, X_val, y_val):.1%}")
```
::::
<!-- NOVEL: needs sign-off -->
This MLP has no layer that behaves differently in training and evaluation, but keep the
`net.eval()` line: it disables training-only behavior such as the dropout mechanism
from @sec-04-training-loss-sgd before evaluation.

The model makes useful predictions on held-out images from the same distribution
as its fitting data. We fixed the split before any experiment, and the separate
test set remains sealed until the end of the chapter. What the validation score
does not establish is whether those predictions respond appropriately when the
spatial arrangement changes.

Before probing the model, separate three questions that are often collapsed into
“the model worked.” Each question needs different evidence.

| Question | Evidence that answers it | What that evidence does not settle |
|---|---|---|
| **Representation:** can the model family express a useful rule? | A construction, approximation argument, or fitted witness | Whether the optimizer will find that rule |
| **Optimization:** did this training procedure reach low empirical risk? | The loss trace, gradients, restarts, and a final training-set check | Behavior on fresh or shifted data |
| **Generalization:** does the fitted procedure work on the distribution we care about? | Independent evaluation drawn from that declared distribution | Performance under an undeclared deployment shift |

: Three claims that require three kinds of evidence. Low training error is evidence
about one optimization run and, indirectly, the available capacity. It is not a
generalization result. {#tbl-three-learning-questions}

## Two experiments that challenge the baseline

### Experiment 1: shift every image two pixels

We take the validation images and shift each one two pixels to the right. This is a
change in position that should preserve the class of a recognizable garment.
Because shifting within a finite frame can also crop the image, we will check
that effect separately. Before you run the cell, predict the accuracy: the model
scores 76% on the original images; what do you expect after the shift?

:::: {.plan-code}
::: {.plan}
1. Define the reusable `shift_right` helper.
2. Shift validation images while keeping the trained MLP fixed.
:::

```{python}
#| label: shift-experiment
#| code-fold: false
# [1]
def shift_right(X: torch.Tensor, px: int) -> torch.Tensor:
    img = X.reshape(-1, 28, 28)
    out = torch.zeros_like(img)
    if px > 0:
        out[:, :, px:] = img[:, :, :-px]
    else:
        out = img.clone()
    return out.reshape(-1, 784)

# [2]
for px in [0, 2]:
    print(f"shift {px}px: validation accuracy "
          f"{accuracy(net, shift_right(X_val, px), y_val):.1%}")
```
::::
After the two-pixel shift, the accuracy falls from 76.0% to 46.5%.

Does the shift fail because it pushes garments off the canvas? Fashion-MNIST scales each
garment's longest edge to fill the frame (Xiao et al.), so wide items such as sandals,
sneakers, and ankle boots reach the right border, and a two-pixel shift crops them.
We measure the crop on its own by zeroing the same two columns without moving
anything.

:::: {.plan-code}
::: {.plan}
1. Measure how much ink the two cropped columns hold.
2. Zero those columns in place, leaving every garment where it was.
3. Print the two ink measurements and the validation accuracy with those columns zeroed.
:::

```{python}
#| label: edge-crop-control
#| code-summary: "Code: separate cropping from moving"
#| code-fold: false
# [1]
edge = X_val.reshape(-1, 28, 28)[:, :, -2:]        # the columns a 2px shift crops
touched = (edge.flatten(1) > 0).any(dim=1).float().mean().item()
ink_share = (edge.sum() / X_val.sum()).item()
# [2]
cropped = X_val.reshape(-1, 28, 28).clone()
cropped[:, :, -2:] = 0
# [3]
print(f"images with ink in the two cropped columns: {touched:.1%}")
print(f"share of all ink in those columns:          {ink_share:.1%}")
print(f"columns zeroed in place, nothing moved:     validation accuracy "
      f"{accuracy(net, cropped.reshape(-1, 784), y_val):.1%}")
```
::::
Removing those columns in place costs two percentage points, far less than the
full shift. The crop-only control therefore does not account for the much larger
loss after displacement.

This is the distinction from @sec-01-linear-regression: validation data drawn from the
data-generating distribution $P$ estimates performance under $P$, not automatically under
a transformed distribution. If $T$ shifts an image while preserving its label, then

$$
R_{T_\#P}(\theta)
=
\E_{(X,Y)\sim P}
\left[\ell\bigl(f_\theta(T(X)),Y\bigr)\right],
$$ {#eq-shifted-risk}

where $T_\#P$ is the distribution obtained by transforming inputs drawn
from $P$ while retaining their labels.
The MLP generalized moderately from its fitting sample to fresh clean examples from
$P$, but it was not robust under $T_\#P$. There is no
contradiction. Clean validation and shift robustness answer different questions. We trained
the model on clean images, then asked it to recognize shifted ones. The loss did not
require robustness to that shift.
@sec-a5-statistical-learning gathers the $P$, $T_\#P$, and deployment-distribution
notation in one place.

As the validation images move right by 0 to 4 pixels, @fig-shift-cliff follows the same
fixed network. We call the resulting drop in accuracy the shift cliff.

:::: {.plan-code}
::: {.plan}
1. Measure validation accuracy at right shifts of 0 to 4 pixels and open the figure.
2. Plot accuracy vs. shift.
:::

```{python}
#| label: fig-shift-cliff
#| fig-alt: "Validation accuracy falls sharply with each additional pixel of right shift, moving from a strong clean score toward the dotted ten-class chance line by four pixels."
#| fig-cap: "Validation accuracy of the clean-trained network under rightward shifts of the validation images. The network is not retrained, and the original labels are retained. The dotted line marks the ten-class chance level; accuracy approaches it by four pixels of shift."
#| code-summary: "Code: accuracy vs. shift"
#| code-fold: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# [1]
shifts = list(range(5))
accs = [accuracy(net, shift_right(X_val, s), y_val) for s in shifts]
plt.figure(figsize=(5.6, 3.3))
# [2]
plt.plot(shifts, accs, "o-", color="#E57200", lw=2, ms=7)
plt.axhline(0.1, ls=":", color="#B8B8A8")
plt.text(0.1, 0.115, "chance (10 classes)", color="#8A8A7A", fontsize=9)
plt.xlabel("shift (pixels right)"); plt.ylabel("validation accuracy")
plt.ylim(0, 0.9); plt.xticks(shifts)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

### Experiment 2: permute the pixel coordinates

We choose one fixed random permutation of the 784 pixel positions and apply it to
*every* image, fitting and validation alike. We keep the original labels attached to
the examples. The displayed arrays are no longer recognizable garments: the ordinary grid
adjacency has been destroyed.

Unlike a small shift, this is not a transformation under which we require the
clean-trained classifier to preserve its decision. A changed prediction after
scrambling is not, by itself, a robustness failure. Nor does the scramble specify
a different correct garment class. Instead, we ask a separate question: can a
fresh model learn the original labels from this consistently re-encoded dataset?
The permutation is invertible, so it changes where information is stored without
removing it. Predict before retraining: does the altered arrangement cost this
MLP five points, twenty, or almost nothing?

:::: {.plan-code}
::: {.plan}
1. Set the seed to 0 and draw `pixel_perm`, a random reordering of the 784 pixel
   positions.
2. Retrain on one fixed permutation of the pixel coordinates.
3. Print validation accuracy for the original MLP and for the retrained MLP on shuffled
   images.
:::

```{python}
#| label: shuffle-experiment
#| code-fold: false
# [1]
torch.manual_seed(0)
pixel_perm = torch.randperm(784)          # one fixed scrambling for all images

# [2]
net_shuffled = train_mlp(X_tr[:, pixel_perm], y_tr)
# [3]
print(f"original images:  validation accuracy {accuracy(net, X_val, y_val):.1%}")
print(f"shuffled pixels:  validation accuracy "
      f"{accuracy(net_shuffled, X_val[:, pixel_perm], y_val):.1%}")
```
::::
The two validation accuracies are close in this one deterministic run. This is
not an uncertainty estimate; it shows that the training recipe can learn a useful
classifier in the scrambled representation.

The two experiments used different protocols. Experiment 1 kept the clean-trained
model and changed only the validation images. Experiment 2 transformed both the
fitting and validation images and retrained.
Complete the other two cells of that two-by-two design:

:::: {.plan-code}
::: {.plan}
1. Evaluate the clean model on scrambled images, without retraining.
2. Retrain the same MLP on shifted images, then evaluate it on shifted images.
3. Print validation accuracy for the scrambled, trained-clean case and the shifted,
   retrained case.
:::

```{python}
#| label: protocol-matrix
#| code-summary: "Code: complete the two-by-two protocol"
#| code-fold: false
# [1]
zero_shot_scramble = accuracy(net, X_val[:, pixel_perm], y_val)
# [2]
net_shifted = train_mlp(shift_right(X_tr, 2), y_tr)
retrained_shift = accuracy(net_shifted, shift_right(X_val, 2), y_val)
# [3]
print(f"scramble, trained clean:     validation accuracy {zero_shot_scramble:.1%}")
print(f"two-pixel shift, retrained:  validation accuracy {retrained_shift:.1%}")
```
::::

## Diagnostic protocol: a fixed model versus retraining

Validation accuracy for the four combinations of transformation and protocol;
the clean-trained model scores 76.0% on untouched validation images. All scores
use the original labels, including those attached to the scrambled inputs.

| Protocol | Two-pixel shift | Fixed pixel scramble |
|---|---|---|
| **Fixed model:** trained clean, evaluated transformed | 46.5% | 8.0% |
| **Retrained:** trained and evaluated on transformed data | 76.5% | 77.0% |

The two results in the first row have different interpretations. The shift result
shows a failure of the desired tolerance to small position changes. The scramble
result shows sensitivity to a much larger change in spatial organization, for which
we did not require invariance. These are not two instances of the same robustness failure.

The second row shows that retraining recovers similar accuracy in both transformed
datasets under this recipe. For the fixed scramble, the next section gives an exact
coordinate-permutation argument. A zero-filled shift also discards boundary pixels,
so its retrained result is empirical, not a consequence of that invertible symmetry.
:::

## Inside the weights: full-frame templates {#inside-the-weights-full-frame-matched-filters}

The distinction between a fitted model and its model family is explicit in the
first layer. Write the fixed scramble as a permutation matrix $\matr{P}$, so a
scrambled image is $\matr{P}\vect{x}$. For any first-layer matrix $\matr{W}_1$,
set $\matr{W}_1' = \matr{W}_1\matr{P}^\top$. Then

$$
\matr{W}_1'(\matr{P}\vect{x})
= \matr{W}_1\matr{P}^\top\matr{P}\vect{x}
= \matr{W}_1\vect{x},
$$ {#eq-permutation-symmetry}

because $\matr{P}^\top\matr{P} = \matr{I}$. With the bias and later layers
unchanged, the entire network produces the same output. Every function this MLP
can compute in the original coordinates has a corresponding parameterization in
the scrambled coordinates.

This is a property of the **model family**, not invariance of one fitted model.
The equation changes the first-layer weights along with the inputs; keeping the
weights fixed does not give the same identity. The initialization is exchangeable
across input coordinates, and Adam applies the same coordinate-wise rule, so the
training procedures correspond in distribution under a fixed permutation
(Exercise 1). Resetting the seed does not itself permute the initial weights,
so the two particular runs need not have identical accuracies.

The dense parameterization therefore gives no built-in preference to the original
pixel adjacency over another ordering. It can still learn spatial regularities
from data; it does not impose locality or translation invariance.

We can inspect that parameterization directly. Each row $\vect{w}_j^\top$ of
$\matr{W}_1\in\mathbb{R}^{256\times784}$ assigns a separate coefficient to every
input pixel. As in @sec-01-linear-regression, it is a **template**
scored by the inner product $\langle\vect{w}_j,\vect{x}\rangle$. Reshaping the row
into a 28×28 image shows its coordinate weights.

:::: {.plan-code}
::: {.plan}
1. Select the largest-norm first-layer templates.
:::

```{python}
#| label: first-layer-template-selection
#| code-summary: "Code: select first-layer templates"
#| code-fold: false
# [1]
W1 = net[0].weight.detach()               # (256, 784)
order = W1.norm(dim=1).argsort(descending=True)[:16]
scale = float(W1[order].abs().max())
```
::::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-templates
#| fig-alt: "Sixteen full-frame weight maps fill a two-by-eight grid. Dark red cells mark positive weights, dark blue cells mark negative weights, and pale cells are near zero; broad diffuse patterns span most of each frame."
#| fig-cap: "Sixteen first-layer weight rows with the largest norms, reshaped into images. The labeled scale runs from negative weights at the blue end through pale zero to positive weights at the red end. Each map shows a separate coefficient for every input pixel; its appearance alone does not establish what the full network recognizes or how robustly it does so."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 8, figsize=(7.6, 2.2))
for ax, i in zip(axes.ravel(), order):
    image = ax.imshow(W1[i].reshape(28, 28), cmap="RdBu_r",
                      vmin=-scale, vmax=scale)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.02, right=0.87, bottom=0.04, top=0.96,
                    wspace=0.05, hspace=0.08)
color_axis = fig.add_axes([0.89, 0.17, 0.018, 0.66])
colorbar = fig.colorbar(image, cax=color_axis)
colorbar.set_ticks([-scale, 0, scale], labels=["negative", "zero", "positive"])
colorbar.ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
plt.show()
```
We should not expect these maps to resolve into edges, contours, or parts that a person
would name, and reading them is subjective. A picture of the weights cannot tell us whether
the network will tolerate a spatial change or fail under it; only a transformation test
can. What the maps do display is the **full-frame parameterization**: each hidden unit
scores the image with an unconstrained template that spans the whole canvas, with an
independent coefficient at every pixel coordinate. The layer contains no compact local
detector that is reused at other positions.

For the pre-activation $z_j(\vect{x})=\vect{w}_j^\top\vect{x}+b_j$, a transformation
$T$ changes the score by

$$
z_j(T(\vect{x}))-z_j(\vect{x})
=\vect{w}_j^\top\bigl(T(\vect{x})-\vect{x}\bigr).
$$

The transformations of interest are **label-preserving**: small shifts of the garment
within the frame, or a symmetry such as the left–right reflection of a shirt, after which
the garment remains recognizable and its class is unchanged. A shift moves each intensity
to a neighboring coordinate, where it is multiplied by a different coefficient, one that
the dense parameterization leaves free of any tie to the first; only training decides how
similar the two are. For a shift of $s$ columns to the right, the ink in the $s$
rightmost columns leaves the frame and changes the score as zeroing those columns in place
would, the crop that Experiment 1 measured on its own. Every other pixel $p$ moves to the
position $p+s$, $s$ columns to its right, and these pixels contribute the rest of the
difference, $\sum_p (w_{j,p+s}-w_{j,p})\,x_p$, with the sum taken over them. The score
change is therefore set by how each coefficient compares with its neighbor $s$ columns
away, a relation the dense layer leaves untied.

Asking each unit's score to stay fixed would be the wrong remedy: for $s=1$ it would
force a template that is constant along every row and blind to horizontal arrangement.
What the dense layer lacks is a unit tied to the shifted copy of $\vect{w}_j$, so that
the response could move with the garment, as the response of a shared local detector does.
A change in one hidden score does not by itself settle the classifier's decision either:
the ReLU and the output layer combine all 256 hidden scores, whose changes can cancel or
accumulate. Tolerance must therefore be measured at the output, as in Experiment 1.

During training, the gradient for row $j$ is a weighted sum of the input images,
$\sum_i\delta_{ij}\,\vect{x}_i$, from the batched form of @eq-bp3.
Adam rescales the coordinates separately, but neither that update nor the
parameterization enforces a compact template or shared coefficients across
positions. Expressive power alone does not supply the particular invariances
we want. We next examine how clean performance changes with capacity.

## Diagnosing the failure: capacity versus geometry

Is the model too flexible, or is the data too sparse for 784 dimensions?

### Capacity: testing the classical U-curve {#capacity-hunting-the-u-curve}

The classical picture, the cartoon of @sec-01-linear-regression, predicts that as
capacity grows, validation error first falls and then *rises* as the model overfits.
A width sweep at two dataset sizes tests that prediction on real data:

:::: {.plan-code}
::: {.plan}
1. Choose the hidden widths to sweep, from 2 up to 256 units.
2. Measure validation error across widths and fitting-set sizes.
:::

```{python}
#| label: width-sweep
#| code-summary: "Code: measure the width sweep"
#| code-fold: false
# [1]
widths = [2, 4, 8, 16, 64, 256]
# [2]
width_errors = {
    n: [1 - accuracy(train_mlp(X_tr[:n], y_tr[:n], hidden=h, epochs=60),
                       X_val, y_val)
        for h in widths]
    for n in (300, 1000)
}
```
::::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-ucurve
#| fig-alt: "Both validation-error curves fall steeply as hidden width increases and then flatten. The smaller fitting set turns slightly upward at the widest models, while the larger fitting set does not."
#| fig-cap: "Testing the classical U-curve: validation error vs. hidden width at two fitting-set sizes. Error falls steeply as capacity grows, then flattens. In this one seeded sweep, n=300 shows a small late upturn while n=1000 does not."
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.5))
for n, color in [(300, "#5379AA"), (1000, "#232D4B")]:
    plt.semilogx(
        widths, width_errors[n], "o-", color=color, label=f"n = {n}", base=2
    )
plt.xlabel("hidden width (capacity)"); plt.ylabel("validation error")
plt.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
The left side of the cartoon appears in both curves: networks with too little capacity
underfit badly. The right side barely appears: a slight upturn at $n = 300$ and a flat
plateau at $n = 1000$. The classical picture predicts a sustained rise in validation
error once the width passes its best value; neither curve shows one. The U is a useful
cartoon, not a law of nature (@sec-01-linear-regression): the optimizer, the sample
size, and the structure of the data can all shape the curve. A
single seeded Adam sweep describes its own regime, so it cannot separate their effects,
estimate a scaling law, or establish a $1/n$ variance law.

The sweep measures **clean validation performance**, not shift robustness. It does
not show that a smaller network would repair the baseline's sensitivity to position:
capacity and the response to a transformation require separate measurements.

### Geometry: the curse of dimensionality

The width sweep leaves the shift failure unexplained, so we turn from the model to the
representation it receives. How informative is distance between raw pixel vectors? Our
images use 784 numbers; a small color image (32×32×3) uses 3,072, a one-megapixel color
photo three million, and a 224×224×3 input 150,528. Covering every combination of
pixel values is out of reach: a grid with 9 values per coordinate contains
$9^2$ points in two dimensions and $9^d$ in $d$ dimensions.

High dimension also erodes the contrast between near and far points:

:::: {.plan-code}
::: {.plan}
1. Fix the seed, list dimensions from 2 to 5000, and start an empty `ratios` list.
2. Measure the nearest-to-farthest distance ratio by dimension.
:::

```{python}
#| label: distance-concentration-audit
#| code-summary: "Code: nearest/farthest ratio versus dimension"
#| code-fold: false
# [1]
torch.manual_seed(6050)
dims = [2, 10, 100, 784, 5000]
ratios = []
# [2]
for d in dims:
    P = torch.rand(300, d)
    D = torch.cdist(P, P)
    ratios.append(((D + torch.eye(300) * 1e9).min(1).values / D.max(1).values).mean())
```
::::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-curse
#| fig-alt: "The average nearest-to-farthest distance ratio rises toward one as dimension increases on a logarithmic horizontal axis. A vertical guide at dimension 784 meets the curve near 0.89."
#| fig-cap: "Distance concentration for 300 points sampled uniformly from a unit cube: the average ratio of nearest-neighbor to farthest-neighbor distance, by ambient dimension. At d=784 the ratio reaches 0.89. This is a controlled geometry example, not a claim that natural images fill the 784-dimensional cube uniformly."
plt.figure(figsize=(5.6, 3.2))
plt.semilogx(dims, ratios, "o-", color="#722F37", lw=2)
plt.axvline(784, ls=":", color="#B8B8A8")
plt.text(830, 0.25, "Fashion-MNIST\n(d = 784)", fontsize=9, color="#8A8A7A")
plt.xlabel("dimension $d$"); plt.ylabel("nearest / farthest distance")
plt.ylim(0, 1); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
In the uniform cube, nearest and farthest distances draw together as the dimension
grows. Natural images are structured and may concentrate
near a much lower-dimensional set, so this is not their empirical distance
distribution. Nor is the $9^d$ grid count a bound on the data needed for translation
tolerance: a translation is described by two numbers, a horizontal and a vertical
offset, not by independent changes to every pixel.

We now measure the pixel geometry of the actual images. How far does a
two-pixel shift carry an image, compared with its distance to the nearest
fitting image?

:::: {.plan-code}
::: {.plan}
1. Measure how far the shift moves each validation image, and how far its nearest
   training image is.
2. Print the share of validation images where `moved` exceeds `nearest`, and both median
   distances.
:::

```{python}
#| label: shift-distance
#| code-summary: "Code: how far does a two-pixel shift move an image?"
#| code-fold: false
# [1]
moved = (X_val - shift_right(X_val, 2)).norm(dim=1)     # (200,)
nearest = torch.cdist(X_val, X_tr).min(dim=1).values    # (200,)
# [2]
print(f"shift moves farther than the nearest training image: "
      f"{(moved > nearest).float().mean().item():.1%} of validation images")
print(f"median distances: shifted copy {moved.median().item():.2f}, "
      f"nearest training image {nearest.median().item():.2f}")
```
::::
In raw pixel space, then, a label-preserving shift can carry an image farther from the
original than the nearest fitting image is. This diagnoses a mismatch between Euclidean
pixel distance and the tolerance the task requires; it does not show that more data or
augmentation cannot improve robustness. We next consider how to build the relevant
structure into training and into the architecture.

## Inductive bias: constraints as knowledge

Recall **inductive bias** from @sec-01-linear-regression: the
assumptions and preferences that distinguish fitted solutions beyond their
agreement with the training sample. Here we have prior knowledge about image
structure and about which position changes should preserve the label. Two
principles suggest how to use it:

1. **Locality.** Nearby pixels jointly form edges, textures, and parts.
   Local connectivity gives these relationships a structural role that the dense
   parameterization does not assign them.
2. **Translation structure.** A local detector's response should move with the feature
   (**equivariance**), while a classifier's final prediction should tolerate or ignore
   small changes in position (**invariance**). The shift experiment tests
   this desired tolerance at the classifier's output.

<!-- NOVEL: needs sign-off -->
### Data augmentation: specifying label-preserving transformations {#data-augmentation-put-the-belief-in-the-examples}

The shift cliff suggests another route. If moving a garment a little should not change
its class, let $T$ be a random label-preserving transformation drawn from a declared
distribution $\mathcal{A}$. The population objective becomes

$$
R_{\mathcal A}(\theta)
=
\E_{(X,Y)\sim P}
\E_{T\sim\mathcal{A}}
\left[\ell\bigl(f_\theta(T(X)),Y\bigr)\right].
$$ {#eq-data-augmentation}

This is **data augmentation**, and its role is larger than making the dataset look
bigger. It is a **data-side inductive bias**: the transformation distribution states
which changes we believe should preserve the target. Sampling shifts from $-3$ to $+3$
pixels says that location within that window is a nuisance. This is an assumption
about the task: complete pixel scrambling is not included in that invariance
requirement. Retraining on one fixed scramble instead changes the encoding of the
whole dataset. The empirical augmented
objective used in training replaces the outer expectation with the sample average.
Drawing one fresh $T$ when an example enters a batch then gives a Monte Carlo estimate
of the inner expectation. Exercise 2 asks you to include those shifts in the training
batches and measure both what the augmentation buys on the shift curve and what it costs on clean
images. @sec-a5-statistical-learning summarizes the corresponding estimators and
distributions.

Augmentation encourages translation tolerance by training on shifted examples.
It does not tie parameters across positions: a dense network still assigns them
separate coefficients. Weight sharing imposes that relation directly. Exercise 2
measures the effect of augmentation with the current MLP; Part II develops the
architectural alternative.

We can now place three familiar levers side by side:

1. **Architecture-side bias** changes which functions are available or easy to learn.
   Local connectivity and shared convolutional filters are the route Part II will take.
2. **Objective- or training-side bias** changes which fitted solution is preferred.
   Weight penalties, dropout, and early stopping from @sec-04-training-loss-sgd are
   examples; the minibatch noise discussed there may also bias which solution training
   reaches.
3. **Data-side bias** changes the examples the model is fitted to.
   Augmentation encodes a chosen family of label-preserving transformations.

These routes can work together, but they are not interchangeable. A finite set
of augmented shifts encourages consistency; it does not prove exact invariance. An
architectural constraint can make a symmetry exact in a layer, but may exclude useful
functions. A penalty prefers some solutions without specifying which input changes
should preserve a label. And augmentation needs a label-preserving transformation:
flipping a garment may be harmless, while flipping a digit or a directional sign may
change the answer.

For Part II we begin with the architecture-side move: **build locality and translation
structure into the network itself** as constraints. Constrain each template to look at
a small local patch instead of the whole frame. Then *share* that template across every
position, so the local detection rule uses the same parameters throughout the image.
These constraints supply locality and sharing; the full classifier's shift tolerance
will still need to be evaluated. The parameter count falls too: our MLP has
203,530 parameters, while the LeNet model in @sec-08-cnn will have 61,706, less than a
third as many.

<!-- NOVEL: needs sign-off -->
::: {.callout-tip}
## Why a constraint can add knowledge

Local connectivity and weight sharing constrain a corresponding dense network
with the same layer sizes. Through @sec-01-linear-regression's
bias–variance lens, we accept assumptions about image structure to reduce the
space of solutions considered. When those assumptions are appropriate, the
restriction can improve data efficiency. The choice remains task-dependent:
we want tolerance to small position changes, not indifference to arbitrary
rearrangements of the pixels. With sufficient data and a suitable training
recipe, architectures with weaker spatial constraints can also perform well,
as Vision Transformers illustrate in @sec-16-vit-scaling.
:::

## Toward local, shared detectors {#the-pivot-toward-local-shared-detectors}

The dense templates of @fig-templates assign separate coefficients across
the whole image. Our next model will instead use **small, local** templates
and apply the **same weights at each position**. Learning a local detection
rule will then determine how that rule is applied elsewhere in the image.

Sliding a local template across the image and scoring each position by an inner
product is a classical operation, decades older than deep learning. Part II opens by
building this operation by hand and then poses the following question:

*What if the template were learnable?*

## One sealed test check

We have now fixed the architecture, optimizer, shift size, and reported metrics. Only now
do we fit the same MLP on all 1,200 development examples and open the 600-example test
set once:

:::: {.plan-code}

1. Run one final test-set check.
2. Print the final model's test accuracy on clean and two-pixel-shifted images.
:::

```{python}
#| label: final-holdout
#| code-summary: "Code: one final test-set check"

# [1]
net_final = train_mlp(X_dev, y_dev)
# [2]
print(f"clean test accuracy:   {accuracy(net_final, X_test, y_test):.1%}")
print(f"shift-2 test accuracy: "
      f"{accuracy(net_final, shift_right(X_test, 2), y_test):.1%}")
```
::::
The sealed check confirms the diagnostic rather than creating it: 80.8% on clean test
images becomes 42.0% after the predeclared two-pixel shift.

Close the book for one minute and test the argument on these three questions.

- Why do we require tolerance to a small shift but not to complete pixel
  scrambling? What separate question does retraining on a fixed scramble answer?

## Okay, so: the missing ingredient is inductive bias

<!-- NOVEL: needs sign-off -->
1. **Clean accuracy and shift robustness are different claims.** The MLP
   predicts well on clean held-out images but loses accuracy after a small,
   label-preserving displacement.
2. **Invariance must match the task.** A complete scramble changes the
   spatial organization and need not preserve a clean-trained model's decision.
   Retraining on that fixed permutation tests learning in a different encoding,
   not invariance of the original classifier.
3. **The model family has a coordinate symmetry.** The reparameterization
   in @eq-permutation-symmetry explains why a dense architecture gives no
   built-in preference to the original pixel ordering. The weight maps display
   its coordinate-specific coefficients; appearance alone does not establish
   robustness or its cause.
4. **Capacity and ambient dimension do not settle the diagnosis.** The
   width sweep describes one clean-data regime, and the uniform-cube example
   illustrates distance concentration under its own distribution. Neither gives
   a general limit on what structured data or augmentation can achieve.
5. **Inductive bias specifies useful structure.** It can enter through
   architecture, objectives, training procedures, or data. Part II develops
   locality and weight sharing; augmentation is a complementary way to specify
   which transformations should preserve the label.

## Deeper dive {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## For the curious: memorization, confidence, and double descent

**Networks can memorize random labels.** Zhang et al. reported 100% training accuracy
on randomly labeled CIFAR-10 and 95.20% on randomly labeled ImageNet under their finite
training budget, not 100% on ImageNet. Capacity is abundant enough that fitting noise
is easy (Exercise 4 reproduces the phenomenon on our subset). Capacity alone therefore
does not explain generalization; the data, optimizer, and architecture must enter the
account.

**Confident far from the data.** A trained ReLU network is piecewise affine:
its input space splits into polyhedral regions, and on each one the logits
$o_k=\vect{w}_k^\top\vect{x}+b_k$ are affine in $\vect{x}$. Along a ray that
remains in one such region, if one logit has a strictly larger slope than the
others, its softmax probability approaches 1 as the distance increases.
Hein, Andriushchenko, and Bitterwolf analyze this behavior for ReLU classifiers.
High softmax confidence therefore need not indicate that an input resembles the
training data. This is a separate question from the label-preserving shift test.

**The bias–variance picture, updated.** Test error can sometimes
*descend again* beyond the interpolation threshold, where the model first becomes
able to fit the training sample exactly: "double descent." The width sweep above does
not establish that pattern. It illustrates why a classical U-shaped curve
should not be assumed in every training regime.

**Further reading**

- Zhang, Bengio, Hardt, Recht, Vinyals,
  ["Understanding deep learning requires rethinking generalization"](https://openreview.net/pdf?id=Sy8gdB9xx)
  (ICLR 2017), the primary source for the random-label experiment.
- Neal,
  ["On the Bias-Variance Tradeoff: Textbooks Need an Update"](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.08286)
  (2019), the source of the "cartoon, not a law" view.
- Belkin et al.,
  ["Reconciling modern machine-learning practice and the classical bias–variance trade-off"](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1903070116)
  (PNAS 2019), a primary account of double descent.
- Hein, Andriushchenko, and Bitterwolf,
  ["Why ReLU networks yield high-confidence predictions far away from the training data and how to mitigate the problem"](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_CVPR_2019/html/Hein_Why_ReLU_Networks_Yield_High-Confidence_Predictions_Far_Away_From_the_CVPR_2019_paper.html)
  (CVPR 2019), the theorem behind confident predictions far from the data.
:::

## Sources and further reading {.unnumbered}

- [Grant Sanderson, *Analyzing Our Neural Network*](https://www.3blue1brown.com/lessons/neural-network-analysis/)
  (3Blue1Brown, 2017; text adaptation by Josh Pullen): a related visual examination
  of first-layer weights and the limits of a trained digit classifier. The
  transformation comparisons here use the Fashion-MNIST model and protocols
  specified in this chapter.
- [Xiao, Rasul, and Vollgraf, *Fashion-MNIST: a Novel Image Dataset for Benchmarking
  Machine Learning Algorithms*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.07747): the benchmark
  dataset used throughout this chapter and several later mechanism studies.
- [Geirhos et al., *Shortcut Learning in Deep Neural Networks*](https://www.nature.com/articles/s42256-020-00257-z):
  a framework for recognizing decision rules that succeed on the benchmark but fail
  at the intended task.
- [Koh et al., *WILDS: A Benchmark of in-the-Wild Distribution Shifts*](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v139/koh21a.html):
  datasets and evaluation protocols that name the deployment distribution rather than
  treating clean validation as a robustness test.
- [Shorten and Khoshgoftaar, *A Survey on Image Data Augmentation for Deep Learning*](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40537-019-0197-0):
  a broad survey of data-side transformations and the invariances they encourage.
- [Bach, *Learning Theory from First Principles*](https://www.di.ens.fr/~fbach/ltfp/):
  develops the formal capacity and generalization tools behind Exercise 6; the
  exercise itself stops at counting.
